title: Russia: politics, society and the strain of a prolonged war
label: 20 October 2026 · Russia inquiry (oral evidence)
summary: Two panels of experts told the Foreign Affairs Committee that Russia has become more militarised, more repressive and economically strained by the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin remains resilient: elites broadly back Putin while parts of the elite and society show increasing unease. Russia has not moved to a full wartime command economy; it is paying for manpower and materiel, creating costly pressures and a growing debt problem. Western sanctions and Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia’s energy revenues, and the UK has underused levers—especially maritime insurance and enforcement—to squeeze Russian export earnings further.

chapters.title: What Russia looks like now
chapters.takeaway: Russia is more militarised and repressive than before, but everyday life in big cities has until recently masked economic strain.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Let's start simply: what is Russia like today for ordinary people?

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Big cities until recently still looked busy—restaurants and shops open—because goods flowed by alternative routes despite sanctions.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: This year changed: Ukrainian strikes reached deep into Russia, hitting refineries and big businesses; household budgets are squeezed and closures are rising.

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: Putin has been in power for 25 years; two generations have known an authoritarian state. The post‑1990s window of pluralism is gone.

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: Socially, many people have reverted to a confrontational mindset—'the West is an enemy'—and repression is high: people jailed for small posts or donations.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Opinion polling shows a big drop in optimism: by August 2026 two‑thirds expected things to get worse—levels not seen since the Soviet collapse era.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So visible normality in cities coexists with growing economic pain and increasing militarisation?

chapters.title: Putinism, elites and the limits of opposition
chapters.takeaway: The regime is resilient, most elites back Putin so long as he seems to be winning, and change is likeliest from elite fractures, not mass revolt.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How resilient is Putin's regime and is 'Putinism' a coherent ideology?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: Very resilient. It rests on a clear worldview: Russia has a special global role, sees the West as unjust, and demands a zone of influence on its borders.

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: Putinism draws on older ideas of Russia as a destined great power; that worldview makes accommodation with the west unlikely without a regime change.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Most of the elite lined up behind the war. They tolerate corruption if the state secures Russia's standing—but they will turn when they think Putin is losing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Where might change come from if not popular uprisings?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: Change will be elite-driven. Russian society is atomised; horizontal organising is weak. If Putin weakens—through health or failures—the elite could shift.

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: I agree change from within the elite is more likely. I am sceptical that foreign-policy moderation will follow without a more fundamental political shift.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: There are pragmatic technocratic factions—Sergey Kiriyenko's circle and his 'New People' movement—who prefer more normal ties with the west, but they'd move only when survival demanded it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Was the Wagner mutiny a model for future coups?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: It set a precedent: it showed rebellion is possible. But a repeat would need a collapse in Putin's grip or a power vacuum.

chapters.title: Society, repression, media and disinformation
chapters.takeaway: The state tightly controls media and political space; disinformation and foreign messaging shape perceptions abroad and inside Russia.

turns.speaker: Fleur Anderson
turns.text: What did the recent Duma elections reveal about control and the opposition?

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: They looked like old patterns—managed outcomes. Notable: Yabloko, the anti‑war liberal party, was barred, showing anxiety about allowing an electoral outlet for opposition.

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: The Kremlin also promoted ex‑combatants into the Duma to legitimise the pro‑war elite, and the presence of many veterans creates new networks the state must manage.

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: The Kremlin runs a huge disinformation effort aimed at weakening western support for Ukraine; it is treated as a key front of the war.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has hitting Russian data centres reduced Kremlin bot activity?

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: No. Short spikes were misread; longer-term trackers show bot activity remains roughly steady. The Kremlin keeps a persistent online influence operation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How can people inside Russia get independent news when the state restricts internet and blocks outlets?

turns.speaker: Abtisam Mohamed
turns.text: Given restrictions, what practical steps can be taken to get independent news to Russians?

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: It's hard. VPNs still work for many but are contested. The UK and allies should invest in Russian-language independent media and technical ways to reach audiences, including in the global south.

turns.speaker: Abtisam Mohamed
turns.text: How credible is Amnesty's reporting that people from low-income countries were trafficked to fight for Russia?

turns.speaker: John Lough
turns.text: It shows the army is short of trained soldiers, so recruiters take desperate steps—sometimes deceptive—to fill ranks, and foreign recruits are part of that.

turns.speaker: Abtisam Mohamed
turns.text: What are prison conditions like for those jailed for dissent?

turns.speaker: Catherine Belton
turns.text: Accounts suggest harsh conditions and severe human-rights violations; for many, prison is brutal and punitive.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does international human-rights pressure matter to the Russian state?

turns.speaker: Dr Deyermond
turns.text: The Kremlin treats human-rights discourse as hypocritical, mirrors allegations against the west, and seeks to confuse global audiences about legitimacy.

chapters.title: The economy: financing the war without full mobilisation
chapters.takeaway: Russia is not a classic command wartime economy: it pays recruits and firms, creating huge fiscal strain, rising debt and a dangerous credit bubble.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is Russia a war economy?

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: It's increasingly militarised but not a full wartime command economy. The state prefers to pay for soldiers and equipment rather than forcibly requisitioning them.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: That choice is expensive: signing bonuses, higher military pay and large payouts to bereaved families make the war pricier and harder to sustain.

turns.speaker: Aphra Brandreth
turns.text: Is the planned record defence allocation for 2027 sustainable?

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: It's a stretch. Much of the rise covers interest on war-related debt; printing and bank credit are propping it up—a risky, Ponzi-like financing that could end badly.

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: Defence is about 40% of federal spending. Russia is funding it by drawing down the National Welfare Fund, raising taxes and cutting services—pressure will grow.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: Russia ran a credit boom to stimulate growth early in the war. That created short-term activity but left a huge corporate debt pile and falling investment.

turns.speaker: Sir John Whittingdale
turns.text: How is the war affecting labour supply and casualty replacement?

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: Russia faces its worst labour shortage ever: battlefield losses plus migration reduce both quantity and quality of recruits, forcing higher wages and worsening inflation.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: That shortage and debt bubble are linked: banks lend to cover wages and losses in defence firms, but capital investment collapses; the state will inherit massive liabilities later.

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: Also note debt servicing is very costly: Russia's annual debt payments are high relative to GDP and expensive compared with other major economies.

chapters.title: Energy, sanctions and where the UK has leverage
chapters.takeaway: Sanctions and Ukrainian attacks have cut Russian energy earnings, but loopholes persist; the UK has underused tools—maritime insurance, enforcement and frozen assets—that could deepen pressure.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How have sanctions and Ukrainian strikes affected Russia's oil and refining?

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: Oil and gas tax revenue fell sharply: in early 2026 the sector's share of budget revenue dropped to about 18% from earlier levels. Refining capacity lost 30–50% in some estimates due to Ukrainian strikes.

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: Russia has had to import diesel and jet fuel because domestic refining was hit; some reported US‑Russia diesel deals may be tiny or undeliverable.

turns.speaker: Richard Foord
turns.text: Do sanctions work overall?

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: They reduce export earnings by 20–30% because Russia must sell at discounts to buyers in India, China and Turkey; but loopholes, the shadow fleet and weak enforcement limit impact.

turns.speaker: Craig Kennedy
turns.text: Targeted actions in 2025—sanctioning key producers and closing refinery loopholes—widened discounts and squeezed revenues. Enforcement and speed matter.

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: The UK and EU should better enforce the price cap, use maritime insurance leverage, reform opaque overseas-territory ownership rules, and coordinate China policy over dual-use tech.

turns.speaker: Alex Ballinger
turns.text: China denies supplying dual-use tech. What actual technologies help Russia's war effort?

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: Many drone components and electronics are sourced via China; there are equity ties and component flows. Diplomacy must link trade talks to consequences for supplies to Russia.

turns.speaker: Isaac Levi
turns.text: The UK can act on maritime services: it insures a large share of coal and LNG shipments. Cutting or taxing those services would hit Russian export receipts and could fund Ukraine reconstruction.

turns.speaker: Dr Gould-Davies
turns.text: Finally, using frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine would hurt the aggressor and help the victim; it is a joint European-level option with big potential effect.
